title: The Role of the Judge in International Trade Regulation
abstract: The WTO is generally seen as a key actor of globalization and, as such, has been the point of convergence of popular irritation worldwide. Many of the reproaches addressed to the WTO show civil societys concern with what is perceived as a democratic deficit in the way the organization operates. The main fear is to see trade rise as the ultimate value, prevailing over concerns such as health and environment. The Role of the Judge offers insight into how disputes are solved at the WTO level, into how the judicial branch interacts with the rest of the organization, and into the degree of sensitivity of the system to external input. The book sheds light on the judicial system governing the WTO and shows it to be the only truly multilateral system where disputes are solved by third-party adjudication. The book develops along three lines: the first a search for cases submitted to the WTO where the judge exceeded its authority; the second a comparison of the WTO with the operations of national judicial systems having different levels of integration, specifically the United States (federal level) and the EC (quasi-federal level); and the third an exploration of directions for the future of dispute settlement in the WTO. Reflecting the diversity of its contributors, this book addresses questions of economics, political science, and law, bringing an unusual level of multidisciplinarity to this topic and context. It is designed for both academic readers and practitioners, who will find it full of practical insights as well as rich and detailed analysis. Thomas Cottier is Professor of European and International Economic Law, University of Bern, and Managing Director, World Trade Institute, University of Bern. Petros C. Mavroidis is Professor of Law, University of Neuchâtel. He formerly worked in the Legal Affairs Division of the World Trade Organization. Patrick Blatter is Mavroidiss scientific collaborator.

Full narrative

The Role of the Judge in International Trade Regulation by Thomas Cottier, Petros Mavroidis and Patrick Blatter was published by University of Michigan Press in 2003. It is part of the Studies in International Economics series. Conceptually, the work connects to Adjudication, Context (archaeology), Political science, Globalization and Convergence (economics).

OpenAlex records 40 citations. That places it in the top 10% of works in its field and year of publication. Citations peaked in 2003 with 18 citing works. Notable citing venues include Cambridge University Press eBooks, Global Constitutionalism and The Journal of Environment & Development. The citing works include 20 book chapters, 7 books, 5 journal articles and 4 dissertations. They come from 8 countries, led by Switzerland, Germany and Australia.

It is recorded in 2 library collections. Its subject matter aligns with Partnerships for the goals among the Sustainable Development Goals.
narrative_llm:
Short impact summary

This 2003 scholarly book has shown clear academic uptake, with 40 citations in OpenAlex and a top-10%-for-year-and-field percentile standing. Its influence is concentrated in research on WTO law, international arbitration and investment law, and broader debates about how trade rules are interpreted and legitimated. The record also points to policy relevance through alignment with SDG 17, Partnerships for the Goals.

Full narrative

The Role of the Judge in International Trade Regulation has established a substantial scholarly footprint in the literature on global trade governance. OpenAlex records 40 citations, and the work is ranked in the top 10% of cited books for its field and publication year. That profile suggests durable academic use rather than a brief surge of attention, with citations continuing across the following years and appearing in later discussions of WTO adjudication, interpretive technique, transparency, and constitutional questions in trade law.

The citing landscape shows that the book is read primarily within international economic law, especially WTO law and international arbitration and investment law. It is cited in a mix of book chapters, books, articles, dissertations, and reference works, indicating that it is used both as a foundational source and as a point of reference in subsequent syntheses and specialized arguments. The most visible citing venues include academic publishers and journals focused on international economic law and constitutionalism, which reinforces the book’s role in core scholarly debates rather than only in peripheral commentary.

The content focus of the citing works also helps explain its continued relevance. Later scholarship draws on the book when discussing the legitimacy and interpretive role of WTO adjudication, the constitutional framing of global trade law, and institutional questions around transparency and appointments. In that sense, the book appears to have helped shape how researchers think about judges and adjudication as part of the architecture of trade regulation, not merely as technical decision-makers.

Beyond citation evidence, the broader record indicates some policy and teaching relevance. Library holdings and subject classifications show that it is catalogued in areas such as international arbitration and foreign trade regulation, supporting its use in research and instruction. The SDG alignment with Partnerships for the Goals is consistent with its subject matter, though the available evidence is strongest for scholarly uptake. Public-event data are unavailable in the current record, so the clearest impact story here is one of sustained academic influence in WTO and international trade law.
